stem:
Tushar lists the factors of three whole numbers: $1$ has only $\{1\}$; $13$ has $\{1,13\}$; $9$ has $\{1,3,9\}$.

How should he classify $1$, $13$, and $9$?

options.text: $1$ is neither prime nor composite, $13$ is prime, and $9$ is composite.
$1$ is prime, $13$ is composite, and $9$ is prime.
The prime, composite, or neither labels are what produce the factor lists $\{1\}$, $\{1,13\}$, and $\{1,3,9\}$.
$9$ is neither prime nor composite because it has the factor $1$.

teacher.key_rationale: 1 has one factor so is neither; 13 has exactly two factors so is prime; 9 has more than two so is composite. Swapping those labels substitutes terms. Saying the labels produce the factor lists reverses the relation. Treating 9 as neither because it has factor 1 misreads the factor-count rule.
